BOOKS AND IDEAS 83
Air Force in 1966 to conduct a scientific study of all available evidence and produce an objective report completely without prejudice.

The Condon Committee report does not conclude that UFOs do not exist. Rather, it concludes that, in general, examination of existing reports and the scientific response indicated that "... UFO phenomena do not offer a fruitful field in which to seek important scientific discoveries." It continues by pointing out that "... what has been obtained from UFO studies over the past 21 years has added nothing to scientific knowledge." At the same time, the committee agrees that "... (scientists) will not accept without criticism our conclusion that the study of UFO reports probably will not advance science." The Committee hoped its report would help scientists "... by identifying the problems and difficulties in addressing them." If scientists disagreed with the report's results, it would be because the report had helped them "... reach a clearer picture of where existing studies were deficient or incomplete and thereby stimulated ideas for more precise studies." The Committee believed that any resulting proposal for clearly defined, specific UFO studies should receive public and private support, since there were scientific areas in which knowledge was incomplete. These "Conclusions and Recommendations" are probably the most important part of the book — manipulation of cases that is not scientific aside — because they are the first (and perhaps the only) thing the reader sees¹. But Jacobs failed to recognize these positive aspects of the Condon Committee report and dwells on its weaknesses, real and supposed.

More importantly for the Air Force, Jacobs fails to understand that the Condon report never led the Air Force to conclude that there were no flying saucers or UFOs. The Air Force and the Condon Committee members who signed the report simply agreed that there was no evidence that UFOs posed a threat to US national security and, therefore, no reason for the Air Force, a defense force, to remain involved in investigating them. The Condon Committee's internal conflict over whether a truly scientific study of the phenomenon was necessary was outside the question of Air Force involvement. Indeed, given the problems that arose over the years, it would probably have been better for another government agency, such as NASA or the FAA, to have undertaken the investigation.

The weak parts of Dr. Jacobs's book are those in which he discusses "contactees," the terrestrial inhabitants with whom space creatures presumably made contact. Gradually, the contacts increased from simple observation to trips to the Moon, Venus, Mars, etc., as each contactee competed to surpass the experiences of predecessors. Jacobs points out that the mission given to these people by the space beings — convincing humankind of the need for peace and brotherhood — is generally a logical response to tumultuous international relations. However, in his critical analysis of these reports, Jacobs is frequently repetitive and disjointed. Although this may result as much from the material he deals with as from his own style, the reader feels this chapter may have been a last-minute addition.

While Jacobs is concerned with the general question of the existence of UFOs, there are other more limited parts of the problem. One area that has figured prominently in flying-saucer lore is the Bermuda Triangle. This area of the Atlantic Ocean, in the triangle between Puerto Rico, Bermuda and Florida, has been the subject of sailors' stories and fears for hundreds of years. About 40 ships and 20 aircraft have been lost there during the past 150 years; some disappeared without a trace. In other cases, crews vanished without an obvious cause from apparently sound ships. A theory developed that this is the operating area not of visitors from outer space but of inhabitants of inner space: a people living underground who venture out in their submarine and aerospace vehicles. Ivan Terence Sanderson advanced this theory in Invisible Residents². There is also another theory that in past ages an advanced people visited Earth and left a homing-type device on the Atlantic seabed, beyond the coastal shelf, to guide future space visitors to Earth.

These two ideas are very frequently considered seriously and accepted without criticism, as in Charles Berlitz's The Bermuda Triangle and John Wallace Spender's Limbo of the Lost³.

Lawrence David Kusche, in The Bermuda Triangle Mystery—SOLVED,† undertakes a critical evaluation of this problem, which has become one part, albeit the smaller one, of the overall question of beings not from Earth versus terrestrial beings. Mr. Kusche is a librarian, not a historian, and his work does not have the same scholarly character as Dr. Jacobs's. One of the greatest obstacles to such a book on this subject is the lack of solid documentation. Newspaper articles and sensational works such as those I mentioned are almost all that is available. Nevertheless, Kusche's book is as valid and important as Jacobs's work, only for those who will discard the myths and emotional interpretations.

Kusche became a reference librarian at Arizona State University in 1972. Frequent requests for information about the Bermuda Triangle led him to discover that little solid information was available. He and a fellow librarian began a lengthy period of correspondence and research with public and private agencies, including correspondence with me about the Air Force's experiences concerning the subject. The result was an extensive bibliography, and further research led Kusche to conclude that many writings had become part of the mystery or legend. Now deeply involved in the subject, Kusche went further to find an answer to the mystery. His background as a reference librarian and aviator gave him a sound basis for researching and understanding the aviation incidents involved. His work differs from an actual history in that he makes no concerted effort to identify the sources of the entries about the legends. LIVROS E IDÉIAS 85
que, como Kusche afirma, “Meu interesse
... é com os próprios incidentes e não
com aqueles que deram publicidade aos
mesmos”.

Qualquer que seja a fonte de atividade,
o mito referente ao Triângulo das Bermudas
tem “crescido” como “Topsy”. Aqueles
que desejam acreditar têm assumido uma
abordagem eclética, modelando — ou, mais
precisamente, remodelando — as estórias
dos desaparecimentos a fim de ajustar
as preconcepções. É essa falsa representação que interessa Kusche. Primeiro ele
apresenta o mito total. Depois apresenta,
em capítulos individuais, o mito de cada
desaparecimento. Em cada caso, o mito é
seguido pelos fatos como conhecidos. Aqui
Kusche fornece as fontes de sua informação.
Em muitos exemplos a adaptação dos fatos
para que estes se ajustem à lenda é imediatamente aparente.

Em outros casos, as revisões têm sido
mais sutis — uma citação fora do contexto
cá, uma pequena declaração cronológica
errônea acolá. Por exemplo, em agosto de
1963 dois aviões tanques KC-135 da Força
Aérea colidiram no ar ao sudoeste de Bermuda. Escombros dessas aeronaves foram
encontrados no dia seguinte. No outro dia,
mais escombros foram encontrados a 160
milhas de distância, mas esses escombros
foram rapidamente identificados como não
tendo conexão alguma com as duas aeronaves. Aqueles que teriam a propensão de
fazer da colisão um mistério convenientemente ignorariam o fato de que os destroços nas duas áreas não se relacionavam de
forma alguma. Ao contrário, questionariam
como, se os dois tanques colidiram, os escombros poderiam estar tão distantes. A
Força Aérea sabia, desde o primeiro dia
da busca, que houvera uma colisão no ar.
Porém, o mito cita “autoridades” não identificadas como coçando suas cabeças e declarando que “algo muito estranho está
acontecendo ali”. Exame lógico dos fatos

reais leva alguém a acreditar que as “autoridades” devem ter sido os laçadores de
cães locais em Yeehaw Junction, Flórida.

Um outro incidente citado em suporte
à lenda envolveu um C-124 da Força Aérea
que “desapareceu” num vôo à “Irlanda”.
Diz a lenda que isso ocorreu em março de
1950, mas a Força Aérea não perdeu C-124
algum naquele mês no Atlântico. Na realidade, a referência parece ser a respeito
de uma aeronave que caiu em março de
1951 a caminho da Inglaterra — e muito
distante do norte do Triângulo. Mais importante, a aeronave não desapareceu.
Dentro de 24 horas de seu acidente — ou
explosão no ar — restos da mesma foram
vistos por um B-29 da Força Aérea. O
navio-aeródromo Coral Sea encontrou o
oceano cheio de debris, alguns dos quais
sua tripulação foi capaz de recuperar e
que foram identificados como oriundos do
C-124. As ondas estavam encapeladas e
havia ventos de tempestade na área, o que
tornou impossível qualquer chance de recuperar corpos.

Talvez o melhor ponto a respeito do
“mistério” do Triângulo das Bermudas foi
apresentado por um oficial da Marinha dos
EUA, citado na revista Time em janeiro de
1975. Ele salientou que o triângulo intensamente trafegado entre as Ilhas de Sabre, os
Açores e a Islândia era a região de muito
mais desaparecimentos inexplicados do que
a do Triângulo das Bermudas⁴. Todavia,
como Kusche ressalta, o Triângulo das
Bermudas é um mistério manufaturado.
Surgiu “devido à pesquisa descuidada e
foi elaborado e perpetuado por escritores
que propositada ou ignoradamente fizeram
uso de falsas concepções, raciocínio falho
e sensacionalismo”. A repetição constante,
então, emprestou à lenda uma aura de autenticidade. Kusche, com sua pesquisa
cuidadosa, tem revelado os elementos de
erro e falsidade envolvendo o mito do
“Triângulo das Bermudas”.

BOOKS AND IDEAS 85
cause, as Kusche states, "My interest ... is in the incidents themselves and not in those who publicized them."

Whatever the source of activity, the myth concerning the Bermuda Triangle has "grown" like "Topsy." Those wishing to believe have adopted an eclectic approach, shaping — or, more precisely, reshaping — the stories of disappearances to fit preconceptions. This misrepresentation is what interests Kusche. First he presents the overall myth. Then, in individual chapters, he presents the myth of each disappearance. In each case the myth is followed by the facts as known. Here Kusche supplies the sources of his information. In many examples the adaptation of facts to fit the legend is immediately apparent.

In other cases the revisions have been subtler — a quotation out of context here, a small incorrect chronological statement there. For example, in August 1963 two Air Force KC-135 tankers collided in midair southwest of Bermuda. Debris from these aircraft was found the following day. On the next day more debris was found 160 miles away, but it was quickly identified as having no connection with the two aircraft. Those inclined to make the collision a mystery would conveniently ignore the fact that the wreckage in the two areas was not related in any way. Instead, they would ask how, if the two tankers collided, the debris could be so far apart. The Air Force knew from the first day of the search that a midair collision had occurred. Yet the myth quotes unidentified "authorities" scratching their heads and declaring that "something very strange is happening there." A logical examination of the actual facts leads one to believe that these "authorities" must have been the local dogcatchers in Yeehaw Junction, Florida.

Another incident cited in support of the legend involved an Air Force C-124 that "disappeared" on a flight to "Ireland." The legend says this occurred in March 1950, but the Air Force did not lose any C-124 in the Atlantic that month. In fact, the reference seems to concern an aircraft that crashed in March 1951 on its way to England — far north of the Triangle. More importantly, the aircraft did not disappear. Within 24 hours of its crash — or midair explosion — debris was sighted by an Air Force B-29. The aircraft carrier Coral Sea found the ocean full of debris, some of which its crew recovered and which was identified as coming from the C-124. The waves were rough and storm winds were blowing in the area, making any chance of recovering bodies impossible.

Perhaps the best point about the Bermuda Triangle "mystery" was made by a US Navy officer quoted in Time magazine in January 1975. He pointed out that the heavily traveled triangle between the Sabre Islands, the Azores and Iceland had far more unexplained disappearances than the Bermuda Triangle⁴. Nevertheless, as Kusche emphasizes, the Bermuda Triangle is a manufactured mystery. It arose "because of careless research and was elaborated and perpetuated by writers who deliberately or ignorantly used misconceptions, faulty reasoning and sensationalism." Constant repetition then lent the legend an aura of authenticity. Through his careful research, Kusche has exposed the elements of error and falsehood surrounding the "Bermuda Triangle" myth.

Seriam aproximadamente 10,00 horas, do dia 27 de outubro de 1973. Ela encontrava-se sózinha em casa, pois nessa ocasião seu espôso havia saído para o trabalho. Da. Sôbre a cintura trazia um cinto com um tipo de fivela desconhecida.
Da. Maria acercou-se do visitante, e, como é natural, perguntou-lhe quem era e o que desejava. Para sua surpresa o "rapaz" disse-lhe que momentos antes estivera no interior da residência à procura de um tipo de rêde que seu filho sabia fazer. Acrescentou ainda, que êle não era daqui da Terra e sim de um outro planeta situado muito além no Espaço, e que o seu objetivo principal ao encontrar-se ali, era para aprender como se fabrica a tal rêde, que se destinaria a ser utilizada nos cestos através dos quais descem de suas naves até o solo.

— EXTRATERRESTRIAL DISAPPEARS BEFORE THE WITNESS —
Mrs. Maria Farias Leivas, 66 years old, married, a resident of Balneário dos Prazeres (Laranjal) in Pelotas, Rio Grande do Sul, told us of the following extraordinary event she witnessed.
It was approximately 10:00 on October 27, 1973. She was alone at home, as her husband had gone to work. Mrs. Maria became somewhat frightened when she heard strange noises inside a room at the back of her home, as if someone were walking there. She distinctly heard footsteps on the floorboards. Food supplies are stored in that part of the house, along with some objects, including hammocks and fishing nets belonging to a married son who lives elsewhere.
Despite her fear, Mrs. Maria went to see what was happening, but no longer saw the intruder. She then went to the front door, and was she not surprised when she looked toward the entrance gate! Standing there was a "strange young man," looking like a student but closely resembling a Japanese person because his "eyes were drawn out to the sides." He must have been 1.50 to 1.60 m tall, with a somewhat slight build. His clothing closely resembled that of a "hippie," but his bluish-gray shirt had designs entirely unfamiliar to the witness, resembling a diamond shape. Around his waist he wore a belt with an unfamiliar type of buckle.
Mrs. Maria approached the visitor and naturally asked who he was and what he wanted. To her surprise, the "young man" said he had been inside the house moments earlier, looking for a type of net her son knew how to make. He added that he was not from Earth but from another planet far out in space, and that his main purpose there was to learn how to make that net, to be used in the baskets in which they descend from their craft to the ground.
Thinking he was merely an impostor trying to make a fool of her, Mrs. Maria told him he had better leave, because she had no time to waste on someone seeking amusement at her expense.
Faced with this impasse, the strange "young man," to prove he was serious, pointed upward and told the woman to watch how "they" descended from the craft, which was not visible. Mrs. Maria then noticed a large, empty basket made of rope or a similar material descending toward the ground, suspended by a rope (see the Canadian case in 1971, Boletim SS&S nº 63, 1972, p. 17). She could not see where the end of the rope supporting the basket was attached. The basket, approximately 2 meters tall, stopped when it touched the ground and then flattened, a few meters from where Mrs. Maria and the "young man" stood.

we witnessed the second event, in the same direction where Carla had seen that light: near the ground, some [ILEGÍVEL] meters from our position, a red light appeared, gradually growing larger and suddenly expanding upward like the flames of an enormous bonfire, to a height of about 10 meters. Its upper part then turned orange, while below, something was rotating with a bright red color, as observed through binoculars. Meanwhile, we noticed a "flash" of white light that occasionally stood out from the larger light, [ILEGÍVEL].

This spectacle of rare beauty, such was the light emitted there, lasted approximately 5 minutes. Afterward, we noticed the orange and red light change to an opaque white, and its size greatly decreased, leaving a triangular shape with its apex pointing upward.

Moments after the curious display had decreased in intensity, I urged my companions to move closer to where the "light" was. Going back about 200 meters along the same path we had previously taken, we parked the cars and positioned ourselves on a rise in the ground, where we could observe the strange luminous phenomenon better and with a wider view. We signaled toward that point several times with our flashlights, including flashing them and tracing angles with the beams, so they would understand that we wanted them to approach us. For a moment, it seemed to us that they were flashing their light. Meanwhile, the orange light had already changed to a dull or opaque white, and beside it, only about 20 meters away, another identical point of light appeared. [ILEGÍVEL]

THEY PICK UP A RADIO TRANSMISSION

We were all naturally euphoric and extremely excited by the dazzling spectacle we were witnessing, so much so that we even forgot to set up the ...-inch telescope, through which we could have better identified that light source.

But, I do not quite know why, the idea came to me of trying to communicate by radio with those intelligences that must have been controlling that luminous display. And so we did. Joined by two others in the group, we began speaking roughly as follows: "Attention! If you really are astronauts from another planet there, please give us an affirmative signal.
